strengths: The task is well motivated: combining a reference person image with a description of changed appearance addresses a useful retrieval setting. ITCPR contributes 2,202 composed queries and a 20,510-image gallery, with manually annotated captions and additional positive-label screening.

Word4Per provides a coherent, practical pipeline using existing person image–text supervision without composed training triplets. The lightweight inversion network and frozen second-stage encoders make the approach relatively accessible.

The gains over simple baselines are substantial. With ViT-L/14, Table I reports 45.91% Rank-1 and 55.63% mAP, compared with 32.02% and 41.83% for fine-tuned image–text averaging. This supports the usefulness of learned composition.

The experiments cover two backbones, supervision choices, training-data quantities, network architectures, prompts, and ensembles. The pipeline diagrams, loss definitions, optimization settings, and runtime measurements provide useful implementation information.
weaknesses: The central comparison with prior methods is confounded. Table I reuses Pic2Word and SEARLE inversion mappings trained with original CLIP parameters alongside fine-tuned encoders, creating a representation mismatch that the caption acknowledges. Word4Per receives compatible domain-specific training. Retraining these baselines with the same encoders and person data is necessary to attribute the reported advantage to the proposed objectives. This matters particularly because pseudo-word composition and SDM/ID fine-tuning largely follow established methods.

The test-only evaluation protocol is insufficiently protected from model selection. ITCPR is designated exclusively for testing, yet architecture and prompt choices are justified using its results in Figure 7 and Table V. No independent validation set or checkpoint-selection protocol is described. Repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are also absent, limiting confidence in smaller differences between loss configurations.

Benchmark annotation reliability needs stronger evidence. The claim that false negatives are eliminated rests on encoder-selected top-k screening, without specifying k, the screening encoder, or an independent completeness audit. Annotator agreement and disagreement resolution are unspecified. Results broken down by source dataset and appearance-change type would clarify robustness beyond the curated, partially overlapping outfits.

Several implementation ambiguities hinder faithful reproduction. Section III-D is unclear about whether ensembling averages pseudo-word embeddings or encoded query embeddings. The text following Table V selects configuration 4, whereas the inference template corresponds to configuration 5. These should be resolved alongside an explicit model-selection protocol.

The explanation that textual supervision suppresses background information is suggestive rather than established. Figure 9 visualizes the frozen encoder upstream of TINet, and Figure 10 supplies only three retrieval examples. Controlled background perturbations or aggregate measurements would better support this proposed mechanism.

The planned dataset release and stated public-security applications need documentation of source-image reuse permissions and privacy safeguards, together with discussion of misidentification and misuse risks. These issues are directly relevant to the proposed person-retrieval capability.
